safety.text: Use things too big to fit in the mouth, like rolled socks, soft toys or big blocks, and check the baskets for small bits.
Keep stairs gated and the floor clear of trip hazards.

why.text: ZERO TO THREE describes fill-and-dump play for 12–24 months, and AAP lists empty containers among simple objects that help toddlers learn how things work.

activities.title: Chunky puzzle or shape sorter
activities.summary: Sit with your toddler and a chunky knob puzzle or big shape sorter, naming each piece as it goes in.

items: Chunky knob puzzle (2–4 pieces) or big shape sorter

supervision.space: Floor or a low table; pieces stay away from a baby who still mouths things.

steps: Choose a puzzle with a few large pieces, or a sorter with two or three simple shapes.
Take the pieces out together and name each one: 'Cow. Moo!'
Let them try to fit pieces; turn one slightly or guide their hand if they're stuck.
adaptations: Younger toddler: start with a single round piece, or just drop shapes into an open box.
Older toddler: more pieces, or ask 'Where's the duck?' before they place it.
Getting frustrated: finish the last piece together, your hand over theirs.
stopCues: Mouthing pieces more than fitting them

safety.text: Follow the age label; knobs and pieces must be firmly attached and too big to fit in the mouth.
Keep the toddler's puzzle pieces out of a baby's reach, and watch what gets handed to the baby.

why.text: HSE lists simple puzzles for 1–2-year-olds as good for hand–eye coordination and problem-solving; CDC suggests naming each piece as it goes in.

activities.title: Feed the teddy
activities.summary: Give your toddler a teddy or doll, a spoon, a cup and a cloth, and take turns pretending to feed it and tuck it in.

notes: Younger toddlers often copy one action; longer pretend stories tend to come later.

items: Teddy or doll
Plastic spoon, cup and bowl
Small cloth or blanket

supervision.space: Floor space anywhere in the room; pretend food only, no real food or drinks.

steps: Sit on the floor with teddy, a spoon, a cup and a cloth.
Show one pretend action, 'Teddy's hungry. Yum!', as you spoon pretend food to teddy.
Hand over the spoon and take turns; follow their ideas, like a drink, a nap or a bump to kiss better.
adaptations: Younger toddler: just one action, a drink from the cup, and lots of copying.
Older toddler: add a second toy and a little story: teddy's bath or teddy's walk.
Talk through the toy: let teddy ask your toddler a question.
stopCues: Asking for real food: a snack cue, not part of the game

safety.text: Pretend food only, with big unbreakable toy dishes; nothing small enough to fit in the mouth.

why.text: AAP says pretend play lets young children try out social roles and builds communication and language; CDC suggests pretend-feeding a stuffed animal and taking turns.

activities.title: Find the hidden toy
activities.summary: Hide a favorite toy with a bit still showing, ask 'Where's teddy?' and give hints until your toddler finds it.

items: A favorite toy
A cushion, cloth or box to hide it under

supervision.space: One child-proofed room; hide things at floor level, never on shelves or furniture they'd climb.

steps: Let your toddler watch you hide a favorite toy under a cushion or cloth, with a bit sticking out.
Ask 'Where's teddy?' and wait; point or give a hint if they need it.
Celebrate the find, then hide it again somewhere new at floor level.
adaptations: Younger toddler: hide it under one cloth right in front of them.
Older toddler: hide it fully out of sight, or hide yourself behind a chair.
Two children: an older sibling does the hiding while you cheer.
stopCues: Upset when they can't find it

safety.text: Hide things at floor level only, and anchor furniture; searching toddlers climb.

why.text: AAP suggests hidden-toy hunts for 12–18-month-olds and describes hide-and-find games as practice with the idea that things still exist out of sight.

activities.title: Sock basket helper
activities.summary: While you sort clean laundry, hand your toddler socks to drop into a basket, then let them push or carry it, thanking them for helping.

items: Clean socks or small towels
Laundry basket

supervision.space: Wherever you fold laundry, away from the iron, detergent and laundry pods.

steps: Sit on the floor with the clean laundry and a basket between you.
Hand over socks one at a time, 'Sock in!', and let them drop or throw them into the basket.
Say thank you, then let them push or carry the basket a short way to a drawer.
adaptations: Younger toddler: in and out of the basket, as many times as they like.
Older toddler: find the matching sock, or make a pile of all the little ones.
Tidy-up version: toys into a box at the end of play, with a clean-up song.
stopCues: Pulling the folded pile apart (a cue to stop, not to scold)

safety.text: Keep detergent, laundry pods and the iron out of sight and reach while your toddler helps.

why.text: CDC suggests letting toddlers help with everyday tasks, such as putting socks or toys in a basket, and praising them for helping.

activities.title: Toddler-led walk
activities.summary: Walk a safe route at your toddler's pace and let them lead, stopping to squat, look and collect a few big leaves.

notes: New walkers manage short stretches; bring a stroller or carrier for the rest.

items: Optional: stroller or carrier for the way home
Optional: a paper bag for leaves

supervision.space: Sidewalks, paths or a park away from traffic; hold hands near roads, driveways and crossings.

steps: Pick a short, safe route on sidewalks, paths or in a park, and bring the stroller for the way back.
Let your toddler set the pace and choose the stops: cracks, bugs, puddles, leaves.
Hold hands near any road, driveway or crossing; let go only on paths away from traffic.
Collect a few big leaves in a bag and keep an eye on what goes into hands and mouths.
adaptations: New walker: walk a few minutes, ride a while, walk again.
Older toddler: copy animals you see, running like a squirrel or flapping like a bird.
Baby too: the baby rides in the stroller or carrier while the toddler walks holding your hand.
stopCues: Tired legs or asking to be carried
Darting toward the road: time to hold hands or ride

safety.text: Hold your toddler's hand near traffic and at crossings; stick to sidewalks or paths and stay off driveways.
Check hands and mouths often: no berries, mushrooms or small stones. Collect big leaves only.
Dress for the weather; in sun use shade, a hat and sunscreen on exposed skin.
Let them out to walk: WHO advises not keeping young children strapped in a stroller for more than an hour at a time.

why.text: AAP suggests child-led walks, saying toddlers practice walking, running, squatting and climbing as they explore; ZERO TO THREE suggests collecting leaves.

activities.title: Toddler area at the playground
activities.summary: Visit a playground's toddler area and stay within arm's reach as your toddler tries low steps, ramps, small slides and bucket swings.

notes: Look for posted age signs; equipment for older children isn't sized for toddlers.

supervision.space: Toddler-sized equipment over soft surfacing; you within arm's reach whenever they're off the ground.

steps: Head for the toddler section: low climbers, ramps, small slides, spring rockers and bucket swings.
Check the ground is soft (mulch, sand or rubber), slides aren't hot, and nothing is tied to the equipment.
Stay within arm's reach on anything off the ground; spot them up the steps and at the slide's end.
Mix in running on the grass and a sit-down break in the shade.
adaptations: New walker: ramps, low steps and the bucket swing, with you in front.
Confident climber: a low ladder and small slide, still with you right there.
Busy playground: go at a quieter time or stay in the fenced toddler area away from running older kids.

safety.text: Use toddler-sized equipment and stay within arm's reach; toddlers need closer supervision than older children.
Touch slides and metal before use; they can burn in the sun. No hood drawstrings, helmets or cords around the neck.
Use shade, a hat and sunscreen on exposed skin; avoid the hottest hours.

why.text: CPSC lists low climbers, ramps, small slides, spring rockers and full-bucket swings as toddler equipment; AAP says outdoor play helps build balance.

activities.title: Scoop-and-pour water tub
activities.summary: Sit right beside your toddler at a shallow basin of water with cups, spoons and a funnel; tip the water out the moment you finish.

items: Shallow basin or washing-up bowl
A little water
Plastic cups, spoons and a funnel
Towels

supervision.space: You within arm's reach the whole time, phone away; towel under the basin; water emptied right after.

steps: Put a shallow basin with just a little water on a towel, indoors or outside.
Sit right beside your toddler, phone away, and hand over cups, spoons and a funnel.
Pour together and name what happens: full, empty, splash, drip.
When you finish, tip the water out straight away and put the basin out of reach.
adaptations: Younger toddler: one cup and one spoon; splashing and grabbing is the game.
Older toddler: add a sponge to squeeze or toys that float and sink.
Baby at home too: do this while the baby sleeps or another adult has them.
stopCues: Putting their face in or drinking the water
Tipping the basin or throwing water

safety.text: Stay within arm's reach with full attention the whole time; toddlers can drown in an inch or two of water.
Empty the basin as soon as play ends; never leave water standing, and an older child can't be the one watching.
Wipe up spills; wet floors are slippery. Outdoors, add shade and a hat.

why.text: HSE lists jugs and a basin for water play for 1–2-year-olds as sensory play that builds hand–eye coordination; CDC and ZERO TO THREE suggest cups, spoons and a funnel.

activities.title: Over, under, in and out
activities.summary: Set up a cushion to crawl over, a table to crawl under and a laundry basket to climb in and out of, saying each word as they go.

items: Floor cushion or pillow
Sturdy table or chair to crawl under
Empty laundry basket

supervision.space: Floor level only, away from stairs and hard edges; table and shelves stable or anchored.

steps: Lay out a floor cushion, then a sturdy table to crawl under, then an empty laundry basket.
Show the way, saying each word: 'Over the cushion... under the table... in the basket... out!'
Stay within arm's reach at the basket, where wobbles are most likely, and go round again.
adaptations: Cautious mover: start with just the cushion and the basket, with you on the far side.
Walking toddler: step over the cushion and walk around the table instead of under it.
Add 'through' with a big cardboard box opened at both ends as a tunnel.
stopCues: Bumping their head under the table

safety.text: Keep everything at floor level, with cushions on the floor and never stacked on sofas, and spot within arm's reach.
Use a sturdy table and anchored furniture; climbing toddlers can pull furniture over.

why.text: ZERO TO THREE describes this over-under-in-out game for 12–24 months and says games like it help toddlers learn word meanings while being active.
